title: Eating: food stalls, restaurants, and Sundanese cooking
title_target: Dahar: warung, rumah makan, jeung masakan Sunda
goal: Order food, describe tastes and cooking methods, and understand Sundanese table manners — including the raw vegetables and chili sauce that go with every meal.
bekal: order at a food stall or restaurant at the right speech level
the names of Sundanese dishes and how they are cooked

dialogs.title: Paguneman — At a Sundanese restaurant
dialogs.intro: Midday at a Sundanese restaurant in Setiabudi. Rani and Sari sit on the floor mats in a *saung*, a little bamboo hut. A waiter comes over with the menu.

lines.speaker: Pelayan:
lines.text: Wilujeng sumping. Badé tuang naon, Téh?
lines.id: Welcome. What would you like to eat?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Abdi mah nasi timbel komplit hiji.
lines.id: One nasi timbel with everything for me.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Abdi… naon nya nu teu lada teuing?
lines.id: And I'll have… what isn't too spicy?
lines.literal: I… what [nya] which not spicy too?

lines.speaker: Pelayan:
lines.text: Aya pepes lauk, Téh. Éta mah teu lada. Atawa ayam bakakak.
lines.id: There's pepes lauk — that's not spicy. Or ayam bakakak.
lines.literal: there-is pepes fish, Téh. that [mah] not spicy. or chicken bakakak.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Pepes lauk waé atuh. Sareng cai hérang.
lines.id: The pepes lauk, then. And plain water.
lines.literal: pepes fish just atuh. and water clear.

lines.speaker: Pelayan:
lines.id: And the lalab? Shall I bring all of it?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Sayuran seger, teu dipasak. Dahar jeung sambel. Wajib, Téh.
lines.id: Fresh vegetables, uncooked. You eat them with sambal. A must.
lines.literal: vegetables fresh, not cooked. eat with sambal. must, Téh.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Atah pisan kitu? Kuring can pernah…

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Cobian heula sakeudik. Ulah loba sambelna, sok lada.
lines.id: Try a little first. Go easy on the sambal, it's hot.
lines.literal: try first a-little. don't much sambal-the, tends spicy.

lines.speaker: Pelayan:
lines.text: Sambelna sambel dadak, Téh. Enggal disayogikeun.
lines.id: It's sambel dadak. We'll have it ready right away.
lines.literal: sambal-the sambal sudden, Téh. right-away prepared.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Engké ari tos ngeunah mah, Téh moal daék dahar tanpa lalab deui.
lines.id: Once you get a taste for it, you'll never want to eat without lalab again.
lines.literal: later when already tasty [mah], Téh won't willing eat without lalab again.

notes: **Lada** = spicy (hot). ⚠️ In Indonesian *lada* is the name of a spice (pepper); in Sundanese it is an adjective. *Teu lada* = not spicy. The Indonesian word *pedas* isn't used.

**Ngeunah** = tasty, delicious. It's the main praise for food, and is also used for comfort in general: *ngeunah saré* = sleeping well. The lemes form is **raos**. The opposite is **teu ngeunah** or **hambar** (bland).
**Atah** = raw. The opposite is **asak** (cooked, ripe). For meat that's half done: *satengah asak*.
**Cai hérang** literally means "clear water" and is plain drinking water — the most common drink order. **Cai téh** = tea, **cai kalapa** = coconut water, **cai jeruk** = fresh orange juice.

**Lalab** (or *lalapan*) is raw vegetables served with sambal, and it isn't a garnish but a fixed part of a Sundanese meal. Typically: cucumber, lemon basil, boiled cassava leaves, small round eggplants, long beans, watercress. Refusing lalab is fine, but you'll be asked why.
**Sambel dadak** = sambal (chili sauce) ground fresh on the spot, in front of you, in a stone mortar. *Dadak* means sudden, made on the spot. It's the mark of a serious Sundanese restaurant.
**Enggal** = right away (lemes); loma: **buru-buru** or **gancang**. *Enggal disayogikeun* = it will be prepared right away.

grammars.title: Cooking methods: one word, one technique
body: Sundanese has a separate verb for almost every way of cooking, and dish names are often taken straight from those verbs. Recognize the pattern and you can read a menu without asking.

head: Verb
Technique
Dish name
Example
rows: to wrap in leaves and steam
to steam in a rice steamer
to cook rice with spices & coconut milk

after: Notice the prefix **N-**, which changes shape to match the first letter of the root: *goréng* → **ngagoréng**, *pais* → **mais**, *kukus* → **ngukus**, *sangu* → **nyangu**. This is how Sundanese forms active verbs, covered fully in Unit 10 — for now, just recognize it.

⚠️ **Pais** and **pepes** are the same word; *pepes* is the form better known outside West Java. In Sundanese-speaking restaurants you'll see *pais lauk* (fish), *pais oncom*, *pais jamur* (mushroom).

blocks.title: Ordering phrases
items: **Badé tuang naon?** — What would you like to eat? (asked of you)
**Abdi badé neda ____.** — I'd like to eat ____. (about yourself)
**Aya naon waé di dieu?** — What do you have here?
**Nu teu lada aya?** — Is there anything that isn't spicy?
**Sambelna misah waé.** — The sambal on the side, please.
**Tambih sangu sakedik.** — A little more rice, please. (*tambih* = add, lemes)
**Sadayana sabaraha?** — How much is it altogether?
**Punten, tiasa bungkus?** — Excuse me, can I get it to take away?

blocks.text: ⚠️ Look again at the golden rule from Unit 3, because it gets tested most at the table. The waiter asks you *badé tuang naon?* — column 3, because you are the one being honored. You answer with column 2: *abdi badé neda…*. Answering *abdi badé tuang* is a mistake everyone will hear at once.

head: Name
What it is
Notes
rows: usually *komplit*: chicken, tofu, tempeh, lalab, sambal
rice cooked with coconut milk & spices
shared, eaten straight from the pot
whole chicken split open and grilled
typical of West Java, found nowhere else
Bandung street food; aromatic ginger (*kencur*) is a must
grated cassava filled with oncom / palm sugar
rice-flour pancake from a clay stove
drunk at night when it's cool

blocks.text: Some Sundanese food names are shortened sentences, and that is part of the fun: **comro** from *oncom di jero* (oncom inside), **misro** from *amis di jero* (sweet inside), **colenak** from *dicocol énak* (tasty when dipped), **cilok** from *aci dicolok* (skewered tapioca), **cireng** from *aci digoréng* (fried tapioca). Once you can take a name apart, you're halfway to understanding the language.

blocks.title: Sundanese table manners
items: **Mangga tuang.** — Please, eat. Said by the host; don't start before you hear it.
**Punten, ti payun.** — Excuse me, I'll go first. Said if you finish before others.
**Tos wareg, hatur nuhun.** — I'm full, thank you. (*wareg* = full)
**Ngeunah pisan!** — Delicious! Praise that is always welcome.
Eating with your right hand, without a spoon — **dahar ku leungeun** — is normal and not rude; Sundanese restaurants even provide a finger bowl for it.
To decline a second helping, **cekap, hatur nuhun** with a smile is enough. Declining twice is taken to mean you really mean it.
